source_evidence.anchor: Section 2.4, paragraph defining the Erdos-Renyi model G(n,p)
source_evidence.observation: The model has n vertices, and every pair of distinct vertices is connected independently with probability p.

source_evidence.anchor: Section 2.4, paragraph defining vertex degree and d
source_evidence.observation: The degree of a vertex is the number of incident edges, and every vertex has expected degree (n - 1)p, denoted d.

There is an absolute constant C such that, for G distributed as G(n,p), the condition d >= C log n implies that, with high probability (for example, 0.9), every vertex has degree between 0.9d and 1.1d.

source_evidence.anchor: Proof of Proposition 2.4.1, fixed-vertex Chernoff step
source_evidence.observation: For a fixed vertex i, its degree d_i is the sum of n - 1 independent Ber(p) edge indicators, so Exercise 2.3.5 gives P{|d_i - d| >= 0.1d} <= 2 exp(-c d) for an absolute constant c > 0.

source_evidence.anchor: Proof of Proposition 2.4.1, union bound and complementary event
source_evidence.observation: The union bound gives P{there exists i <= n with |d_i - d| >= 0.1d} <= sum_{i=1}^n P{|d_i - d| >= 0.1d} <= 2n exp(-c d). For d >= C log n and C sufficiently large, this is at most 0.1, hence P{for every i <= n, |d_i - d| < 0.1d} >= 0.9.

source_evidence.anchor: Exercise 2.3.5 (Chernoff's inequality: small deviations), cross-referenced in the proof
source_evidence.observation: In the setting of Theorem 2.3.1, for a sum S_N of independent Bernoulli variables with mean mu and delta in (0,1], P{|S_N - mu| >= delta mu} <= 2 exp(-c mu delta^2), where c > 0 is absolute.

binders: There exists an absolute constant C, chosen sufficiently large and independent of n and p [PDF page 10, printed page 21, Proposition 2.4.1; PDF page 11, printed page 22, final proof paragraph].
The graph-size parameter n is the number of vertices, and p is the common edge probability in the Erdos-Renyi model G(n,p) [PDF page 10, printed page 21, opening definition of G(n,p)].

G is a random graph distributed according to G(n,p), and the probability in the conclusion is over this random graph [PDF page 10, printed page 21, Proposition 2.4.1 and the preceding model definition].
Vertices are indexed by i with i <= n in the proof, and d_i denotes the degree of vertex i [PDF page 10, printed page 21, proof opening; PDF page 11, printed page 22, union-bound display].
hypotheses: G is sampled from the Erdos-Renyi model G(n,p), in which every pair of distinct vertices is connected independently with probability p [PDF page 10, printed page 21, opening definition and Proposition 2.4.1].
The common expected vertex degree d = (n - 1)p satisfies d >= C log n [PDF page 10, printed page 21, expected-degree display and Proposition 2.4.1].
conclusions: With probability at least 0.9, all vertices simultaneously have degrees within 10 percent of d; the proof states the event exactly as: for every i <= n, |d_i - d| < 0.1d [PDF page 11, printed page 22, final probability display].

Equivalently for the proof's strict event, with probability at least 0.9 every d_i satisfies 0.9d < d_i < 1.1d; the proposition's prose says the degrees are 'between 0.9d and 1.1d' [PDF page 10, printed page 21, Proposition 2.4.1; PDF page 11, printed page 22, final display].

The proof establishes the quantitative failure bound P{there exists i <= n such that |d_i - d| >= 0.1d} <= 2n exp(-c d), which is at most 0.1 when C is sufficiently large under d >= C log n [PDF page 11, printed page 22, union-bound display and following paragraph].
definitions_and_conventions: G(n,p) is the random graph on n vertices obtained by connecting every pair of distinct vertices independently with probability p [PDF page 10, printed page 21, opening definition].
The degree of a vertex is the number of edges incident to that vertex [PDF page 10, printed page 21, degree definition].
d := (n - 1)p is the expected degree of every vertex [PDF page 10, printed page 21, expected-degree display].
For a fixed vertex i, d_i is a sum of n - 1 independent Ber(p) random variables, namely the indicators of the edges incident to i [PDF page 10, printed page 21, proof opening].

The small-deviation Chernoff estimate used in the proof has an absolute constant c > 0 and is applied with mean mu = d and relative deviation delta = 0.1 [PDF page 9, printed page 20, Exercise 2.3.5; PDF page 10, printed page 21, Chernoff display].
implicit_context: The surrounding construction is the usual finite Erdos-Renyi graph on n vertices: edges correspond to pairs of distinct vertices and there are no loop indicators in a vertex degree [PDF page 10, printed page 21, model definition and the count of n - 1 incident Ber(p) indicators].

As a probability parameter, p is implicitly admissible as a Bernoulli probability, while n is implicitly an admissible finite vertex count; Proposition 2.4.1 does not restate exact endpoint or lower-bound conventions for these parameters [PDF page 10, printed page 21, model definition and proposition].

Independence is required among the n - 1 incident edge indicators for each fixed vertex; the proof does not assume that the degrees d_i of different vertices are independent, since it passes from fixed i to all i using a union bound [PDF page 10, printed page 21, fixed-vertex step; PDF page 11, printed page 22, union-bound step].

semantic_facets.topic: Quantifier order and uniformity of constants
details: The existential absolute constant C precedes the choice of the random graph parameters; it is not allowed to depend on n, p, G, or the vertex i [PDF page 10, printed page 21, first two sentences of Proposition 2.4.1].

The proof also uses an absolute Chernoff constant c > 0 and then chooses C sufficiently large relative to it [PDF page 9, printed page 20, Exercise 2.3.5; PDF page 11, printed page 22, paragraph after the union bound].

The conclusion concerns every vertex in one sampled graph simultaneously, not one fixed vertex and not merely an expectation [PDF page 10, printed page 21, proposition conclusion; PDF page 11, printed page 22, complementary-event display].
The fixed-vertex estimate is lifted to the simultaneous event by summing over all n vertices with the union bound [PDF page 11, printed page 22, union-bound display].
The numerical success probability certified in the passage is at least 0.9, equivalently failure probability at most 0.1 [PDF page 11, printed page 22, final two paragraphs and display].
Before specializing to 0.9, the proof obtains the exponentially decaying failure upper bound 2n exp(-c d) [PDF page 11, printed page 22, union-bound display].
The relative tolerance is exactly 0.1d around the expected degree d [PDF page 10, printed page 21, proposition and fixed-vertex estimate].

The proof's success event uses strict inequality |d_i - d| < 0.1d because its failure event uses >=; this corresponds to strict bounds 0.9d < d_i < 1.1d [PDF page 11, printed page 22, union-bound and complementary-event displays].
The result is about degrees in the Erdos-Renyi random graph G(n,p), with independent edges of common probability p [PDF page 10, printed page 21, model definition].
The centering value d is not an arbitrary parameter: it is fixed to the common expected degree (n - 1)p [PDF page 10, printed page 21, expected-degree display].

undebatable_constraints: C is one absolute constant uniform in the graph parameters, and the density premise is d >= C log n [PDF page 10, printed page 21, Proposition 2.4.1].
The graph distribution is G(n,p), with every pair of distinct vertices connected independently with probability p [PDF page 10, printed page 21, model definition and proposition].
The comparison value is exactly the common expected degree d = (n - 1)p [PDF page 10, printed page 21, expected-degree display].
The claim controls every vertex simultaneously, not merely a fixed or randomly selected vertex [PDF page 10, printed page 21, proposition conclusion; PDF page 11, printed page 22, universal event].
The certified probability level is at least 0.9, with failure probability at most 0.1 [PDF page 11, printed page 22, final proof paragraph and display].
The proof's exact success event is |d_i - d| < 0.1d for all i, and its exact failure estimate is at most 2n exp(-c d) [PDF page 11, printed page 22, union-bound and complementary-event displays].
The fixed-vertex Chernoff step relies on d_i being a sum of n - 1 independent Ber(p) edge indicators [PDF page 10, printed page 21, proof opening].

ambiguities.issue: The proposition's word 'between' does not by itself specify whether the endpoint bounds 0.9d and 1.1d are inclusive.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 10, printed page 21, Proposition 2.4.1 says 'between 0.9d and 1.1d', while PDF page 11, printed page 22, the proof states the complementary event as |d_i - d| < 0.1d.
ambiguities.impact: A formal statement using non-strict bounds matches the natural inclusive reading of the prose but is slightly weaker than the strict event explicitly proved; endpoint strictness should therefore be compared explicitly.

ambiguities.issue: The exact admissible range for n and the convention for log are not restated in Proposition 2.4.1.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 10, printed page 21, introduces n as a vertex count, p as a probability, and writes d >= C log n without an explicit lower bound on n or an explicit logarithm-base declaration in the selected passage.
ambiguities.impact: Ordinary nondegenerate graph parameters and the standard logarithm convention are clearly intended, but a formalization's treatment of n = 0 or n = 1, or its chosen logarithm normalization, may require contextual reconciliation rather than being attributed to an explicit clause of the proposition.

ambiguities.issue: The phrase 'with high probability (for example, 0.9)' mixes qualitative terminology with one concrete confidence level.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 10, printed page 21, Proposition 2.4.1 uses that phrase; PDF page 11, printed page 22, the proof concretely derives success probability at least 0.9 after choosing C sufficiently large.
ambiguities.impact: The unambiguous quantitative contract supplied by this passage is the at-least-0.9 statement. A stronger asymptotic interpretation of 'with high probability' is not expressly quantified in Proposition 2.4.1 and should not be silently substituted.

contract_plain_english: There is a universal absolute constant C such that an Erdos-Renyi random graph G(n,p), whose n vertices have common expected degree d = (n - 1)p, has all vertex degrees simultaneously within 10 percent of d with probability at least 0.9 whenever d >= C log n [PDF page 10, printed page 21, Proposition 2.4.1; PDF page 11, printed page 22, final display]. For each fixed vertex its degree is a sum of n - 1 independent Ber(p) edge indicators, so the cited small-deviation Chernoff inequality gives failure probability at most 2 exp(-c d); a union bound over all n vertices gives total failure probability at most 2n exp(-c d), which is at most 0.1 for sufficiently large C [PDF page 9, printed page 20, Exercise 2.3.5; PDF pages 10-11, printed pages 21-22, proof]. The proof's exact successful event is strict, |d_i - d| < 0.1d for every vertex, although the proposition itself uses the potentially inclusive word 'between' [PDF pages 10-11, printed pages 21-22].
